_doc: T-3645: the 1812 person cards' stories (data/residents_1812/stories.json) retold for younger readers. Keyed by person id; each age a list of paragraphs, one for each of the story's own. The story itself is read at the age it measures, and by everyone older (tools/reading_levels.py); only the younger ages are written here, and the story itself is never rewritten. No fact enters that the story does not hold; for readers of 8-10 the worst of the fighting is told plainly but without its gore (Kevin's 1812 rulings: the student jaunts keep to the build-up and the aftermath).

8-10: Black Partridge was a Potawatomi chief. In his own language his name was Muck-otey-pokee. His village was on the Illinois River, across from the top of Peoria Lake. In 1795 General Wayne gave him an American medal at a treaty meeting. For seventeen years he kept his word to the Americans.

On the night of 14 August 1812 he went to see Captain Heald, with a man to turn his words into English. He gave the medal back. He said he could not hold back the young men. Birds had been singing in his ears, he said. The next morning he was painted for war. He found Margaret Helm, who was seventeen, in the water at the edge of the lake. He pulled her out of the fight and led her safely to the camp. On the 16th he sat on the Kinzies' porch to guard them. He took Mrs. Lee and her baby home to his village.

In the war that came next, his own village was wiped out in one day. A writer named Andreas tells that he later set Lieutenant Helm free. He paid the Kankakee people with his pony, his gun and the gold ring he wore in his nose.

Black Bird was called Mucketepennese by his own people. The French called him Letourneau. He was the Potawatomi war leader on 15 August 1812. That spring he was counted with Pepper's band on the Au Sable River. The year before, he had met with the Americans at Peoria.

When the fight on the sand hill was over, Captain Heald walked out alone toward the warriors. Black Bird came to meet him, with a man to turn his words into English. He asked Heald to give up. He promised that the prisoners would not be killed. Heald gave up. A writer named Quaife thought Black Bird's father was the chief who helped the Americans attack St. Joseph in 1781.
Thomas Burns had been a soldier at the fort. When his time was done, he stayed. He built a house on the north bank of the river. He married a widow, Mrs. Cooper, and raised her children as his own.

In April 1812 people were killed at Lee's farm. After that, Heald made the men of the town into a small army called the militia. Burns was put in charge of them, as their sergeant. On 15 August he marched out with the twelve men. He was badly hurt in the fight. About an hour after the Americans gave up, he was killed where he lay.

Mrs. Burns was once called Mrs. Cooper. Then she married Thomas Burns. She brought a house full of kids to his home on the north bank. In April 1812, people were killed at Lee's farm, and everyone ran to the fort. She had had a baby just the day before. The Kinzies carried her to the boat on her bed, with the new baby in her arms.

On 15 August she lost her husband. She lost her son Joseph and two more of her kids too. She and her girls were taken prisoner. They lived with the Indians for two years. Then traders paid to get them back at Mackinac and sent them to Detroit. By 1820 she lived in Detroit. Her husband was gone, and she worked hard to raise her three kids who lived.

Joseph Cooper was the son of Mrs. Burns from her first marriage. Some stories call him James. Thomas Burns was his stepdad. In April 1812 Heald made the men of the town into a small army called the militia. Joseph joined it with his stepdad.
On 15 August he marched out with the militia. All twelve of them were killed that morning. Joseph was one of them.

Isabella Cooper was about nine in the summer of 1812. She was a daughter of Mrs. Burns from her first marriage. On 15 August a warrior grabbed her. She was only a child, but she fought back as hard as she could. She was badly hurt on her head. An old woman of the camp saved her life.

She was a prisoner for two years with her mom and sister. In 1816 she went to live with the Edwards family in Detroit. They remembered that at thirteen she still had the scar. She grew up and married a man named Farnum. She lived in Detroit for many years.
The Burns baby was born in April 1812. The very next day, everyone ran to the fort to be safe. Her mom held her on her bed as they carried them onto the Kinzie boat.

After 15 August, when she was a prisoner, she was hit by a hatchet, and she lived. Twenty-two years later, a young woman walked up to Juliette Kinzie on a steamboat. She said her name. She lifted the hair from her forehead and showed the scar.
This was another of Mrs. Burns's young kids. No one wrote down the child's name. In the spring of 1812 the family left their house on the north bank to be safe in the fort.
On 15 August the wagon with the children of the fort was attacked. Mrs. Burns's two kids who came after Isabella died there. This child was one of them.

Billy Caldwell was also called Sauganash. That means "the Englishman." He was born around 1780. His mom was Potawatomi, and his dad was a British officer born in Ireland. In 1812 he rode with Tecumseh and the British. All the old stories agree he was not at Chicago when the soldiers marched out.

A book by Juliette Kinzie, called Wau-Bun, tells it this way. He came across the river by canoe on the 16th. Just then, angry warriors from the Wabash came to the Kinzie house. He talked them down and saved the family. Later he led the joined bands at the treaty of 1833. He went west with them in 1836. He died at Council Bluffs in 1841.
11-13: Billy Caldwell was called Sauganash, which means "the Englishman." He was born about 1780. His mother was Potawatomi, and his father was a British officer born in Ireland. In 1812 he rode with Tecumseh and the British. The old accounts agree that he was not at Chicago when the soldiers marched out.

Juliette Kinzie's book Wau-Bun brings him across the river by canoe on the 16th. Just then a war party from the Wabash came to the Kinzie house in an angry mood. In her story he talks them down and saves the family. Later he led the joined bands at the treaty of 1833. He went west with them in 1836 and died at Council Bluffs in 1841.

8-10: He was one of the Chicago militia, the small army of men from the town. No one wrote down his name. He lived in the little town. He may have worked for a trader, or he may have been a Frenchman from the river. He picked up a gun when the fort asked for men.

In April 1812 people were killed at Lee's farm. After that, Heald signed up fifteen men of the town. Three ran away. Twelve marched out on 15 August, and all twelve were killed. We know only a few of their names. He stands here for one of the men who were counted but never named.

Fielding Corbin was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He served five full years in the army, left, and then came back. He signed up again in October 1811. In the summer of 1812 he was at Fort Dearborn with his wife.

On 15 August his wife was killed in the fight. She was going to have a baby soon. He was taken prisoner. Two years later he was one of nine men from the fort who came home by way of Quebec. They got to Plattsburg, New York, in May 1814.
Mrs. Corbin was married to Fielding Corbin, a soldier. She lived with him at the fort. The book Wau-Bun says she told everyone from the start that she would never let the enemy take her.

On 15 August she kept her word. She was going to have a baby soon. She fought, she would not be taken, and she was killed. A later story calls her Sukey Corbin, and says she washed clothes at the fort. But even Kirkland, the writer who printed that story, did not trust it as much as the older ones.

Louis Fettle came from French Canada. Some stories spell his name Pettell. He lived at Chicago with his Indian wife before the soldiers came to build the fort in 1803. His name shows up in John Kinzie's money books every year until 1812.
Then it stops. A writer named Quaife thought he marched with the militia on 15 August and died with them. In this town he lives in one of the old log houses on the north bank, near the Kinzies.

This was a child from the fort. No one wrote down the child's name. On 15 August eighteen children rode out with the soldiers, in a covered wagon behind them. We know the families of eleven. The rest, like this child, were only counted.

This child most likely came from a soldier's family or a family from the town. It may have been the Lees, the Burnses, the Holts or the Needses. The wagon was attacked in the fight, and twelve of the children died.

Otho Hays was a sergeant, a soldier in charge of other soldiers. He joined in April 1811. Every story of the fight says he was one of the bravest men in Heald's company. One of the warriors who knew the fort was Nau-non-gee, a chief from the Calumet village. Hays had been kind to him many times.

On 15 August the two men met in the fight. John Kinzie first told the story to Henry Schoolcraft in 1820. He said each man gave the other a deadly wound at the same moment. Hays died there. Nau-non-gee died a few days later at his village.
John Crozier was a sergeant, a soldier in charge of other soldiers. He had been at Fort Dearborn since July 1808. He was one of the old hands of the company.

He lived through the fight on 15 August. He was taken as a prisoner to the Au Sable River. There a Chippewa man, an old friend, took him away to Green Bay and set him free. Lieutenant Helm made a list of the soldiers who lived. By mistake, he wrote that Crozier had run away. But Crozier was one of the sergeants alive at Detroit that fall.

William Griffith lived in the town. He was not a soldier until April 1812, when people were killed at Lee's farm. On 1 May he joined the army right here at Chicago. Soon he was a sergeant. Later it was Griffith who told how Black Partridge gave a warning. Birds had been singing in his ears, the chief said.

On 15 August Topenebe, the chief from St. Joseph, took him prisoner. Then he let Griffith hide. Griffith got away by canoe to Mackinac with Captain and Mrs. Heald. He went home with them by way of Detroit and Pittsburgh. Eight years later he wrote to Heald. He wanted to help Mrs. Burns get money from the army, since her husband had died.

Thomas Forth was a corporal, a soldier with a small rank. He joined in July 1807 for five years. His time ran out on 6 July 1812, five weeks before the soldiers left the fort. No record says he signed up again. But he was still counted among the men who marched out.
No list of the men who lived has his name. So he is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight on the morning of 15 August.

Joseph Bowen was a corporal, a soldier with a small rank. He joined the company in April 1811. He lived through the fight on 15 August. The Fox River people took him, and he lived with them as a prisoner for about nine months.

Someone paid to get him back at Chicago. He was sent by way of Amherstburg to Quebec, and got there in November 1813. In May 1814 he was one of nine Fort Dearborn men who made it to Plattsburg, New York.

George Burnett played the fife for the company. A fife is a small flute. He had been a soldier since 1806, and he signed up again in July 1811. His fife marked each part of the soldiers' day. It played when they woke up, when they lined up, and at the evening gun.
No list of the men who lived has his name. So he is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight on the morning of 15 August.

John Smith was the younger of two John Smiths. He was one of the company's two fife players. A fife is a small flute. His dad, also named John Smith, was a soldier in the same company. They joined three years apart and lived in the same barracks.
Both lived through 15 August. The younger Smith is counted with the men who made it home.
Hugh McPherson played the drum for Heald's company. He joined in October 1807. The man who copied the list made a mistake. It said he would serve until 1852!
No list of the men who lived has his name. So he is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight on the morning of 15 August.

John Hamilton was the second drummer. He had been at Fort Dearborn since July 1808. The drums told the soldiers what to do all day. The book Wau-Bun says the band played a sad song, the Dead March, as the soldiers marched out of the gate on 15 August.
No list of the men who lived has his name. So he is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight on the morning of 15 August.
John Allin was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. An older list spells his name Allen. He joined in November 1810. He came out to the fort with Heald's company.
No list of the men who lived has his name. So he is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight on the morning of 15 August.
George Adams was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He first joined in 1806. He signed up again in August 1811. He had been at the fort a long time.
No list of the men who lived has his name. So he is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight on the morning of 15 August.
Prestly Andrews was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He first joined in 1806. In December 1810 the list said he was sick. He signed up again in April 1811.
Lieutenant Helm wrote that he was killed in the fight on 15 August. He is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died there.
James Corbin was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He joined in October 1810. Fielding Corbin was in the same company. No record says if they were family.

He lived through the fight and the long time as a prisoner after it. Two years later he was one of nine men from the fort who came home by way of Quebec. They got to Plattsburg, New York, in May 1814.
Asa Campbell joined the army in January 1810. By the end of that year he was a corporal, a soldier with a small rank. By the spring of 1812 he was a plain private again.
No list of the men who lived has his name. So he is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight on the morning of 15 August.
Dyson Dyer was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He joined in October 1810. In December the list said he was sick.

Lieutenant Helm wrote that he was killed on 15 August. But Dyer was alive. He was a prisoner. Two years later he was one of nine men from the fort who came home by way of Quebec. They got to Plattsburg, New York, in May 1814.
11-13: Private Dyson Dyer joined the army in October 1810. That December, the list of soldiers said he was sick.

Lieutenant Helm wrote him down as killed on 15 August. But Dyer was alive, a prisoner. Two years later he was one of the nine men of the fort who came home from captivity by way of Quebec. They reached Plattsburg, New York, in May 1814.

8-10: Stephen Draper was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He had been in the army since 1806. He signed up again in April 1811.
No list of the men who lived has his name. So he is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight on the morning of 15 August.
Daniel Daugherty joined the army in August 1807. His time was almost up in 1812, and war was coming. So on 1 June 1812 he signed up again.
He lived through the fight on 15 August. He was alive at Detroit that October. A man named Woodward listed him with the soldiers who lived.
Micajah Denison was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He joined in January 1811.
He was hurt very badly on 15 August. A man named Woodward wrote that he was not likely to live. That night five of the hurt prisoners were killed in the camp. People think he was one of them.
Nathan Edson was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He joined in April 1810.
He was taken prisoner on 15 August, and he lived. Two years later he was one of nine men from the fort who came home by way of Quebec. They got to Plattsburg, New York, in May 1814.

Paul Grummo signed up for five years in October 1810. In the spring of 1812 he was a soldier in Heald's company at Fort Dearborn. Long after, he said he spent that summer as a scout. He said he carried messages through the woods between Fort Dearborn and Fort Wayne.

He said he was taken in the fight on 15 August. He said a chief took him in as family, even though Paul had killed the chief's son. He said the chief took him far to the north-west, past the Falls of St. Anthony, and then sold him to the British near Detroit. However it really happened, he was one of nine men from the fort who came home by way of Quebec. They got to Plattsburg in May 1814.

He made his home at Maumee City, near Toledo. There he went by Paul De Garmo. He was a tall, strong man, and he always said he had been at Fort Dearborn. But the army had him down as a man who ran away, so he never got his soldier's money. A writer named Quaife says he stretched the truth, like old soldiers do. The records show he joined and served. The adventures are his own story.
Richard Garner joined the army in October 1810. By that December he was a corporal, a soldier with a small rank. By 1812 he was a plain private again.

He lived through the fight on 15 August. But that night, five hurt prisoners were killed in the camp, and he was one of them. A man named Woodward could find out only two of their names. Garner's was one.
William Nelson Hunt came from Maryland. He joined the army in October 1810.
He lived through the fight and was taken away as a prisoner. That winter he froze to death.
Nathan A. Hurtt was one of the newest men in the company. He joined in December 1811.
Helm's list of the men who lived has a name that is hard to read. It may be Hurtt's, or it may be William Hunt's. If it is Hunt's, then Hurtt was one of the twenty-six soldiers who died on 15 August.
Rodias Jones joined the army in December 1807. In 1810 he was a corporal, a soldier with a small rank. In 1812 he was a plain private again. He had seven months left to serve.
No list of the men who lived has his name. So he is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight on the morning of 15 August.
David Kennison joined the army in March 1808. He was at Fort Dearborn, ready for duty, in May 1812. He said he was born in New Hampshire in 1736. That would have made him seventy-six that summer!

He came home from the war. When he was very old, he came back to Chicago. He died there on 24 February 1852. He was buried in the City Cemetery, which is now Lincoln Park. In 1905 a big rock was put there to remember him.
Samuel Kilpatrick signed up again in December 1810. The 1810 list spells his name Kirkpatrick.
No list of the men who lived has his name. So he is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight on the morning of 15 August.

John Kelso had served his time and left the army in December 1810. On 6 April 1812 he was at Lee's farm, on the South Branch of the river. A war party came and killed the two men there. Kelso and a boy got away. They ran to the fort to warn everyone.

Four weeks later, on 3 May, he joined the army again at Chicago. No list of the men who lived has his name. So he is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight on the morning of 15 August.
Jacob Landon joined the army in November 1807. The 1810 list said he was not fit to serve. But he was still with the company in 1812.
No list of the men who lived has his name. So he is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight on the morning of 15 August.
Michael Lynch was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He signed up again in December 1810.
He was hurt badly on 15 August and taken prisoner. He was killed on the march, before they got to the Au Sable River.
Hugh Logan came from Ireland. He had been a soldier since 1806. He signed up again in February 1811.
He lived through the fight and was marched away as a prisoner. When he grew too tired to walk any more, he was killed.
Frederick Locker was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He joined in April 1810.
No list of the men who lived has his name. So he is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight on the morning of 15 August.
Peter Miller had been a soldier since 1806. In 1810 the list said he was there but not fit to serve. He signed up again in July 1811.
No list of the men who lived has his name. So he is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight on the morning of 15 August.
Duncan McCarty was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He joined in August 1807. His time was to end two weeks after the soldiers left the fort.
He lived through the fight and his time as a prisoner. A man named Woodward listed him with the men still alive that fall.
William Moffett was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He signed up again in January 1811. In this town he walks at the front of the fort's wagon with Elias Mills.
No list of the men who lived has his name. So he is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight on the morning of 15 August.
Elias Mills was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He joined in October 1811. He was one of the younger men of the company. In this town he leads the fort's wagon with William Moffett.
He lived through the fight and his time as a prisoner. Two years later he was one of nine men from the fort who came home by way of Quebec. They got to Plattsburg, New York, in May 1814.
Joseph Noles was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. The newspapers spelled his name Knowles. He joined in September 1810.
He lived through the fight and his time as a prisoner. Two years later he was one of nine men from the fort who came home by way of Quebec. They got to Plattsburg, New York, in May 1814.

He lived through the fight and the long time as a prisoner after it. Two years later he was one of the nine men of the fort who came home by way of Quebec. They reached Plattsburg, New York, in May 1814.

8-10: Thomas Poindexter was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He joined in September 1810. In May 1812 the list said he was sick.
He was hurt and taken prisoner on 15 August. That night five hurt prisoners were killed in the camp. People think he was one of them.
William Prickett was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He joined in March 1811.
No list of the men who lived has his name. So he is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight on the morning of 15 August.
Frederick Peterson was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He joined in June 1808.
No list of the men who lived has his name. So he is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight on the morning of 15 August.
David Sherror was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He joined in October 1810.
No list of the men who lived has his name. So he is counted with the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight on the morning of 15 August.
John Suttenfield was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He joined in September 1807. His time was to end three weeks after the soldiers left the fort.
He was hurt badly on 15 August and taken prisoner. He was killed on the march, before they got to the Au Sable River.
James Starr was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He joined in November 1809.
Lieutenant Helm wrote that he was killed on 15 August. He was one of the twenty-six soldiers who died in the fight.
James Van Horn was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He joined in May 1810. That December, the list said he was sick.
He lived through the fight and his time as a prisoner. Two years later he was one of nine men from the fort who came home by way of Quebec. They got to Plattsburg, New York, in May 1814.

Nathan Heald was a captain. He was born in New Ipswich, New Hampshire, in 1775. From 1810 he was in charge of Fort Dearborn. In May 1811 he married Rebekah Wells in Kentucky. They rode back to Chicago on horseback with Cicely, the woman who worked for her.

In August 1812 General Hull told him to give up the fort. Heald gave the store's goods to the Potawatomi who had come. He wrecked the extra guns and poured out the liquor. On the morning of 15 August he marched out along the lake shore toward Fort Wayne. With him were fifty-four soldiers, twelve men of the town, and the families. A mile and a half south, they were attacked. Heald was shot in the leg and the arm. He gave up to Black Bird, who promised the prisoners would not be killed.

He and Rebekah were taken to St. Joseph. They got away by canoe to Mackinac. Then they went home by way of Detroit, Buffalo and Pittsburgh. He was made a major. He left the army in 1814, when it was made smaller. He made his home in St. Charles County, Missouri, and died there in 1832. No picture of him is left.

Rebekah Wells was born in Kentucky in 1790. Her dad was General Samuel Wells. Her uncle was Captain William Wells of Fort Wayne. She married Nathan Heald in May 1811, when she was twenty. She rode the long way to Chicago on horseback.

In May 1812 her first baby, a boy, was born dead. There was no one at the fort skilled at helping babies be born. On 15 August she rode out with the soldiers on a horse. She was hurt six or seven times. A warrior held her. Jean Baptiste Chandonnai saved her life. He paid with a mule and a promise of whiskey. Then he brought her back to her husband. Together they got away to Mackinac and home to Kentucky. She died in Missouri around 1857.

Cicely was enslaved by the Healds. That means they owned her and she was not free. She came with them from Louisville on horseback in June 1811. The old records give her only this one name. She lived in the captain's house the whole year and a half the Healds were at the fort. Her baby son lived with her.

On 15 August she and her son were killed in the fight. Years later, Rebekah Heald asked to be paid for what her family lost. She wrote that John Kinzie had once offered six hundred dollars for Cicely.
Cicely's baby boy lived with his mother in the captain's house. No record gives his name or his father's name.
He was killed with his mother on 15 August. He was one of the twelve children who died that morning.

Linai T. Helm was a lieutenant, an officer. He came to Fort Dearborn from Detroit. He was the company's second lieutenant. He married Margaret McKillip. She was seventeen, and John Kinzie was her stepdad.

On 15 August a gun shot hit his right foot. He was taken prisoner and carried down the Illinois River. A trader named Thomas Forsyth got him back for two horses and a keg of whiskey. He reached the Americans at St. Louis on 14 October. In March 1813 he found his wife again at his dad's house in New York. In 1814 he wrote down what happened in the fight. Few men who were there ever did.
11-13: Lieutenant Linai T. Helm came to Fort Dearborn from Detroit. He was the company's second lieutenant. He married Margaret McKillip, John Kinzie's stepdaughter, who was seventeen.

On 15 August a bullet hit his right foot. He was taken prisoner and carried down the Illinois River. The trader Thomas Forsyth paid two mares and a keg of whiskey to get him back. He reached the Americans at St. Louis on 14 October. In March 1813 he found his wife again at his father's house in New York. He wrote his own story of the massacre in 1814. It is one of the few written by a man who was there.

8-10: Margaret Helm was the daughter of Eleanor Kinzie and her first husband, a British officer named McKillip. In the summer of 1812 she was seventeen. She was the young wife of Lieutenant Helm.

On 15 August she rode out with the soldiers. Twenty years later, Juliette Kinzie wrote down her story in the book Wau-Bun. A warrior grabbed her. She fought her way toward the lake and was pulled into the water. The man who saved her was Black Partridge. He led her to the camp. She was taken across to her mom's house. She went with the Kinzies to St. Joseph and Detroit. In March 1813 she got to her husband's family in New York, a week before he did.
11-13: Margaret Helm was the daughter of Eleanor Kinzie and her first husband, a British officer named McKillip. She was seventeen in the summer of 1812, and the young wife of Lieutenant Helm.

On 15 August she rode out with the soldiers. Juliette Kinzie wrote down her story in Wau-Bun twenty years later. It tells how a warrior grabbed her, how she fought toward the lake and was pulled into the water, and how the man who saved her was Black Partridge. He led her to the camp. She was taken across to her mother's house. She went with the Kinzies to St. Joseph and Detroit, and in March 1813 she reached her husband's family in New York a week before he did.

8-10: Matthew Irwin ran the government's store at Chicago. From 1809 he kept the trading house outside the fort. He sold goods to the Potawatomi at fair prices. The idea was to win them away from the British traders.

On the evening of 17 June 1812 he stood a short way off. He saw the whole fight in which John Kinzie killed Lalime, a man who turned Indian words into English. On 5 July he closed the store. He gave the keys to Dr. Van Voorhis and left Chicago for good.
11-13: Matthew Irwin was the United States factor at Chicago. From 1809 he kept the government trading house outside the fort. He sold goods to the Potawatomi at fair prices, to win them away from the British traders.

On the evening of 17 June 1812 he stood twenty or thirty yards away. He saw the whole fight in which John Kinzie killed Lalime, the interpreter. On 5 July he closed the storehouse, gave the keys to Dr. Van Voorhis and left Chicago for good.

8-10: Kee-po-tah was a Potawatomi chief. He was a friend of the Kinzie family. He was visiting them when General Harrison came by, and they met there.

On 15 August he and another man guarded the Kinzie boat at the mouth of the river. The fight went on down the shore. On the 16th he sat with the guards on the Kinzies' porch. In November he took the family safely to Detroit. He was still with them there the next fall.
11-13: Kee-po-tah was a Potawatomi chief and a friend of the Kinzie family. He had been visiting them when General Harrison came through and met him there.

On 15 August he and another man guarded the Kinzie boat at the river mouth, while the battle was fought down the shore. On the 16th he sat with the guards on the Kinzies' porch. In November he took the family safely to Detroit, and he was still with them there the next fall.

8-10: He was one of John Kinzie's boatmen. He came from French Canada, or was part French and part Indian. No one wrote down his name. Kinzie's men lived in a house next to his. Each day they ate a quart of corn and a little fat. They rowed the boats and worked with the furs.

In the fall they went out to the places where they spent the winter. In the spring they came back with bundles of furs. So they were at Chicago from May. They worked hard all day. In the evening they laughed, sang and told stories. On 15 August a boatman rowed the Kinzie boat at the mouth of the river. On the 18th he took the family to St. Joseph.

He was another of John Kinzie's hired men. He came from French Canada, or was part French and part Indian. No one wrote down his name. The book Wau-Bun talks about "the boatmen" in the Kinzie boat on 15 August. The house for the Frenchmen held more than one man.
Like the other hired men, he spent the winter far out, and came back with the furs in the spring. On 15 August he was with the family in the boat. On the 18th he helped take them to St. Joseph.

John Kinzie was born in Quebec in 1763. First he learned to make things out of silver. Then he started trading with the Indians. He came to Chicago around 1804. He took the old house on the north bank of the river, across from the fort. He grew to be the most important trader there.

He knew everyone, and everyone knew him. On 12 August 1812, Heald met with the chiefs, and Kinzie turned their words into English. Two months before, on the evening of 17 June, he had fought Jean Lalime outside the fort's gate. Lalime turned Indian words into English for the army. Kinzie killed him. A friend took Kinzie to Milwaukee that night, until it was safe to come back.

On 15 August Topenebe warned him what was coming. Kinzie put his family in the boat. Then he marched out with the soldiers himself. His friends among the chiefs kept him alive. In the days after, he and his family were spared. They were taken to St. Joseph and Detroit.

Eleanor Kinzie was born Eleanor Lytle. Her first husband had died. She was Mrs. McKillip then, and she had a daughter, Margaret. Around 1800 she married John Kinzie. They had four children. She ran the big house across the river.

From April 1812 the family lived inside the fort. On the morning of 15 August she sat in the boat at the mouth of the river. Her four younger kids and their nurse were with her. She watched her husband and her oldest daughter march away with the soldiers. They both came back to her alive. The family spent three worried days at the house across the river. Then they were taken to St. Joseph and Detroit as prisoners of war.
John Harris Kinzie was born at Sandwich, in Canada, in July 1803. In the summer of 1812 he was nine. He was the oldest child of John and Eleanor Kinzie.

On 15 August he sat in the family boat at the mouth of the river. His mom, his sisters and his baby brother were with him. The fight went on down the shore. He went with the family to St. Joseph and Detroit. When he grew up, he worked with the Indians for the government. He helped start the city of Chicago. His wife, Juliette, wrote a book called Wau-Bun. It told the family's story.
11-13: John Harris Kinzie was born at Sandwich, in Canada, in July 1803. He was nine in the summer of 1812, the oldest child of John and Eleanor Kinzie.

On 15 August he sat in the family boat at the river mouth with his mother, sisters and baby brother, while the battle was fought down the shore. He went with the family to St. Joseph and Detroit. He grew up to be an Indian agent and one of the founders of the city of Chicago. His wife Juliette wrote Wau-Bun, the book that told the family's story.

8-10: Ellen Marion Kinzie was born in Chicago in December 1805. She was one of the first children born to a family that lived there. In the summer of 1812 she was six and a half.

She was in the boat with her mom on 15 August. She went with the family to St. Joseph and Detroit. When she grew up, she married Dr. Alexander Wolcott. He worked with the Indians at Chicago for the government.
Maria Indiana Kinzie was born in Chicago in 1807. In the summer of 1812 she was about four.
She was in the boat with her mom on 15 August. She went with the family to St. Joseph and Detroit. When she grew up, she married David Hunter. Later he was a general in the Civil War.
Robert Allen Kinzie was born on 8 February 1810. He was the baby of the family. In the summer of 1812 he was two and a half.
He was in his mom's arms in the boat on 15 August. He went with the family to St. Joseph and Detroit. He came back to Chicago as a young man. He traded there in the 1830s.
Josette LaFramboise was a young woman. Her family was French and Ottawa. She was the nurse who cared for the Kinzie kids. (The man who printed Wau-Bun got her name wrong. He called her Grutte.)

On 15 August she sat in the boat with Mrs. Kinzie and the kids while the fight went on. Soon after, she married Jean Baptiste Beaubien. Some stories say it was in 1812, and some say 1814. As Madame Beaubien, she raised a big family in Chicago in the 1830s.

Jean Baptiste Chandonnai was John Kinzie's clerk. He was a young man from a French and Potawatomi family. He was at home both in the trading house and in the camps. On 15 August Kinzie left his family in Chandonnai's care in the boat.

That same day he saved Rebekah Heald. She was hurt, and a warrior was about to kill her. Chandonnai paid for her life with a mule and a promise of whiskey. He brought her back to her husband. Then he took the Healds toward St. Joseph. Every story of that day says he worked and worked to save the prisoners.
That fall he took Mrs. Kinzie and the kids to Detroit. By about 1816 he was working for Kinzie again. He traded at Chicago and farther away. At the treaty of 1821 he was given two big pieces of land.

Pierre Le Clerc worked for John Kinzie. The book Wau-Bun calls him Peresh. He was a young man from a French and Indian family. He had lived a few steps from the fort for years. One story says he was the one who brought the news of war to Chicago in July.

On 15 August he marched with the soldiers and fought on their side. Then Helm asked him to go over to the warriors. He carried the words about giving up back and forth between the two sides. He lived. At the treaty of 1821 he was given a piece of land on the Elkhart River.

Jean Lalime worked for the army at Fort Dearborn. He turned Indian words into English. He was a Frenchman who had gone to school. He spent winters at Chicago from 1803, in one of the log houses on the north bank. The fort's doctor called him a very nice man and a good friend. His letters to Fort Wayne passed on what the Indians were saying.

At sunset on 17 June 1812, the fort's gate was being shut. He and John Kinzie met just outside it and fought. Kinzie was cut on the neck, and Lalime was killed. He was buried near the Kinzie house, inside a fence, where people on the porch could see.

Charles Lee came to live at Chicago around 1805. People say he had the job of bringing food to the soldiers. His farm was on the South Branch of the river. It was called Lee's Place, and later Hardscrabble. It fed the fort. His family lived in a house near the mouth of the river.

On 6 April 1812 a war party killed the two men working on the farm. Everyone in the town ran into the fort. That spring Lee joined the small army of town men, called the militia. On 15 August he and his son were killed with the rest of the twelve.

Mrs. Lee lived with her husband, Charles, and their kids in the house near the mouth of the river. On 15 August she lost her husband, her son, and her daughter, who was twelve. Black Partridge took her and her baby to his village as prisoners.
That winter a trader named Du Pin paid to get her and her baby back at Chicago. In time Mrs. Lee married him and became Madame Du Pin. People say she sold the Lee house to Jean Baptiste Beaubien.
The Lees' daughter was about twelve in the summer of 1812. Black Partridge was very fond of her.
On 15 August she rode out on a horse with the soldiers. The book Wau-Bun says she was badly hurt. Black Partridge could not save her. So he ended her pain himself.
This was the Lees' baby, the youngest of the family. No record keeps the baby's name.
The baby was taken prisoner with its mom on 15 August. The baby got sick but lived. That winter someone paid to get them both back at Chicago.
Liberty White was an American. He had lived at Chicago for a while. He was in charge of Charles Lee's farm on the South Branch of the river.
On 6 April 1812, a little before sunset, some strangers came to the farm. They killed him and a Canadian man, Jean Baptiste Cardin. The news sent every family in the town running into the fort.
11-13: Liberty White was an American who had lived at Chicago for some time. He was in charge of Charles Lee's farm on the South Branch.

A little before sunset on 6 April 1812, a party of strangers who had come to the farm killed him and the Canadian Jean Baptiste Cardin. His body had been shot twice and stabbed many times. The news sent every family in the town into the fort.

8-10: Jean Baptiste Cardin came from Canada. He had come to Chicago not long before. In the spring of 1812 he worked on Lee's farm. One April day some visitors came to the farm. He said he could tell from their clothes and face paint that they were not Potawatomi.
He was right to be worried. A little before sunset on 6 April, they killed him and Liberty White.
Fox Running was a runner. He was sent by Main Poc, a Potawatomi war leader who had joined the British.
He came into the camp at Chicago on 14 August 1812. He carried a big red belt. It was the sign of war. He brought news that the British were winning up north.
Jean Baptiste Mirandeau was a Frenchman. His wife was Ottawa. His daughter remembered him as a smart and very handsome man with lots of books. He was one of the first people to settle at Milwaukee.

In 1811 he came down to Chicago and worked as a blacksmith at the fort. His family stayed in the Ouilmette house across the river. On the night of 17 June 1812, John Kinzie killed Lalime. Mirandeau packed a few things and took Kinzie to Milwaukee. His family went home too. They were gone before the fort burned.

Victoire Mirandeau was born around 1800. Her dad was the blacksmith Jean Baptiste Mirandeau. Her mom was Ottawa. She grew up speaking French and her mom's language. She never learned to read or write.

In 1811 the family came down from Milwaukee. They stayed at the Ouilmette house while her dad worked at the fort. At sunset on 17 June 1812, the gates were being shut. She and her sister Madeline watched John Kinzie and Lalime fight. That night her dad took Kinzie to Milwaukee, and the family went too. Years later she lived with the Kinzies and worked for them.
Madeline Mirandeau was a daughter of the blacksmith. His name was Jean Baptiste Mirandeau. Her mom was Ottawa. Later she married John K. Clark.

She stayed at the Ouilmette house with her family while her dad worked at the fort. At sunset on 17 June 1812, she and her sister Victoire saw John Kinzie and Lalime fight. The family left that night. She lived at Chicago before the big fight and after it, but not when it happened.

Nau-non-gee was one of the chiefs of the Calumet village, south of Chicago. The book Wau-Bun remembers something he said that spring. He watched the officers' wives playing. He said they were having lots of fun. But soon, he said, they would be hoeing in his cornfield.

On 15 August he looked for Sergeant Otho Hays, a man who had been kind to him many times. They fought. Each gave the other a deadly wound at the same moment. Nau-non-gee was carried home. He died a few days later.
John Needs was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He came from Virginia. He joined in July 1808. He lived at the fort with his wife and their child.
He lived through the fight on 15 August. But he died as a prisoner, in the middle of January 1813. His wife and child died too.
Nuscotnemeg was called the Mad Sturgeon. He was a Potawatomi war leader. People already blamed him for killings in Illinois in 1810. His daughter was Billy Caldwell's wife.

He was one of the attackers on 15 August. He was badly hurt. By the next day his friends were carrying him off toward the Des Plaines River. He got well. In 1817 a traveler named Storrow met him at Chicago.

Antoine Ouilmette came from French Canada. He said he came to Chicago in 1790, before there was a fort. His wife, Archange, was Potawatomi. When the soldiers came in 1803, they lived in one of the four log houses. He worked for John Kinzie. He carried goods over the land between the rivers.

He never joined the militia. When the soldiers marched out, he just stayed home. The Kinzie boat left on the 18th. After that he was the only white man left at Chicago. He was still there, living calmly, when new soldiers came in 1816. In 1829 his wife was given land at Gros Point. The town there, Wilmette, is named after him.
Archange Ouilmette was a Potawatomi woman. One story calls her Okra. She was married to Antoine Ouilmette. The house she ran on the north bank was part of the Kinzie place.

On the morning of 15 August she stood by her house and watched the soldiers march out along the shore. Her family stayed through all that came after. In 1829 a treaty gave her and her children land. Later she went west with her people. She died at Council Bluffs.
Mrs. Bisson was Archange Ouilmette's sister. She lived in the Ouilmette house on the north bank.
The Kinzie family told this story. On 16 August she hid Margaret Helm in the Ouilmette house. Warriors came and searched the room. She sat calmly on the bed, sewing, the whole time.

These are the children of Antoine and Archange Ouilmette. They grew up in the house on the north bank. They spoke French and Potawatomi. Their names were Elizabeth, Michell, Lewis, Francis, Sophie, Joseph and, later, Josette. No one wrote the names down until long after.
They stayed at Chicago with their mom and dad through the massacre and the war. Very few people did that. When they grew up, they went west to Kansas with the Potawatomi.
11-13: These are the children of Antoine and Archange Ouilmette. They grew up in the house on the north bank, speaking French and Potawatomi. Their names were Elizabeth, Michell, Lewis, Francis, Sophie, Joseph and, later, Josette. They were written down only long afterwards.
They stayed at Chicago with their parents through the massacre and the war. They were among the very few who did. As grown-ups they went west with the Potawatomi to Kansas.

8-10: Pee-so-tum was a Potawatomi warrior. He was at the big gathering in August 1812.
After the fight, he led Margaret Helm toward the lodges. She remembered what he held in his hand. She knew by its black ribbon that it was from Captain Wells, and that Wells was dead.

Alexander Robinson was also called Che-che-pin-qua. He was a trader from St. Joseph. He was born at Mackinac. His mom was Odawa and his dad was from Scotland. The old stories argue about whether he was at Chicago on 15 August. They all agree on what he did after.

At St. Joseph he took care of the Kinzies. He and his wife paddled the hurt Healds all the way to Mackinac. Later he became a chief of the Potawatomi, Chippewa and Ottawa together. He signed the treaty of 1833. He kept some land on the Des Plaines River, and he died there in 1872.
11-13: Alexander Robinson, called Che-che-pin-qua, was a trader from St. Joseph. He was born at Mackinac to an Odawa mother and a Scottish father. The old accounts argue about whether he was at Chicago on 15 August. They all agree on what he did after.

At St. Joseph he sheltered the Kinzies. With his wife, he paddled the wounded Healds all the way to Mackinac. He later became a chief of the united Potawatomi, Chippewa and Ottawa. He signed the treaty of 1833, kept land on the Des Plaines River, and died there in 1872.

8-10: George Ronan was an ensign, the lowest kind of officer. He came straight from West Point, the army's school, in March 1811. He was the youngest officer at Fort Dearborn. His name is on an order from November 1811. It gave each man a small cup of whiskey.
On 15 August he was killed near the wagons. The book Wau-Bun says he kept fighting to the end, down on one knee.
Shabbona was born Ottawa. He married into a Potawatomi band of the Illinois River and became its leader. In 1812 he was a helper to Tecumseh.

He said he set out for Chicago when he heard the warriors had gone there. He came in with twenty-two men a few hours after the fight. That night he stood with the guards around the Kinzie house. In 1816 he signed the treaty that gave up the land around Chicago. In 1832 he kept the peace. He was given land at Shabbona Grove, but he lost it. He died near Morris, Illinois, in 1859.
11-13: Shabbona was born Ottawa. He married into a Potawatomi band of the Illinois River and became its leader. In 1812 he was a helper to Tecumseh.

By his own story, he set out for Chicago when he heard the warriors had gone there. He came in with twenty-two men a few hours after the fight, and that night he stood with the guards around the Kinzie house. He signed the treaty of 1816 that gave up the land around Chicago. He kept the peace in 1832. He was given land at Shabbona Grove and lost it, and he died near Morris, Illinois, in 1859.

8-10: John Simmons was a private, the plainest kind of soldier. He joined in March 1810. He lived at the fort with his wife, Susan, and their two kids. David was about two. Baby Susan was born at the fort in February 1812.
On 15 August he was one of a small group of soldiers who died fighting around the wagons. His son David was killed in the children's wagon.
Susan Millhouse Simmons came from Pennsylvania. She was married to John Simmons, a soldier. She lived with him at the fort, with their son David and their baby girl.

On 15 August she lost her husband and her son. She carried her baby and walked with the people who held her prisoner. They went to Green Bay, back past Chicago to Mackinac, and on to Detroit. In April 1813 she finally got to her mom and dad's home near Piqua, Ohio. She died in Springville, Iowa, in 1857.
Susan Simmons was born at Fort Dearborn in February 1812. Her dad was John Simmons, a soldier. Her mom was also named Susan.

On 15 August she was six months old. Her mom carried her the whole time they were prisoners, and all the way home to Ohio. She lived longer than anyone else who was there that day. She died at Santa Ana, California, on 27 April 1900.
Topenebe was the top chief of the St. Joseph band of Potawatomi. He had been a friend of the Kinzies for many years. His sister, KawKeemee, married a trader named William Burnett.

Early on 15 August he sent word to John Kinzie about what was coming. He kept the Kinzie boat at the mouth of the river, so the family stayed out of the fight. He took Sergeant Griffith prisoner and then let him hide. He kept the Kinzies safe at St. Joseph until November. At the treaty of 1821 he was almost eighty.

Isaac Van Voorhis came from Fishkill, New York. He was the fort's young doctor. In 1811 he was twenty-two. That year he wrote home about the land and how it might grow. When Irwin left in July 1812, Van Voorhis kept the keys to the government store.
On 15 August he was killed near the wagons.
Wau-bee-nee-mah was a Potawatomi chief from the Illinois River. His lodge stood in the camp by the creek.
On 15 August Margaret Helm was brought to the camp. A hurt prisoner was being killed there. The chief hung a mat between two poles so she would not have to see it.
Rain After Thunder was the wife of Wau-bee-nee-mah. She was from the Illinois River band. The book Wau-Bun does not give her a name. We gave her this one.

On 15 August Margaret Helm was brought to the camp. She was shaking and very thirsty. This woman took a kettle and got water from the stream. She stirred in maple sugar with her hand and gave it to her to drink.

William Wells was born in Kentucky. When he was a boy, the Miami people took him. They raised him as one of their own. He married a daughter of Little Turtle, their great war chief. He had fought on both sides in the Indian wars. He worked with the Indians for the government at Fort Wayne. He was Rebekah Heald's uncle.

In August 1812 he rode to Chicago with a band of Miami warriors. He came to lead the soldiers safely to Fort Wayne. He got there on the 13th. On the 15th he led the soldiers out with his face painted black. He was killed in the fight. The warriors honored how brave he was.
Winnemeg was a Potawatomi chief of the St. Joseph River. His name means the Catfish. He was a friend of the Americans. In 1810 he kept his people from joining Tecumseh's side.

In August 1812 he carried General Hull's letter. It told the soldiers to leave the fort. Through Kinzie, he told Heald to go right away. The book Wau-Bun says that on 15 August he and Waubansee tried to save Wells, who was hurt.
11-13: Winnemeg, the Catfish, was a Potawatomi chief of the St. Joseph River. He was a friend of the Americans, and in 1810 he kept his people out of Tecumseh's alliance.

In August 1812 he carried General Hull's letter ordering the soldiers to leave the fort. Through Kinzie, he urged Heald to go at once. On 15 August, Wau-Bun heard, he and Waubansee tried to save the wounded Wells.
